logline: In a near-future Britain where androids called Synths do domestic labour, a family discovers their new Synth carries secret memories - and the question of what counts as consciousness begins to cost people everything.

renewal.note: Channel 4 announced in May 2019 that a fourth series would not be commissioned. The show concluded after three series with the societal implications of Synth consciousness left deliberately unresolved.

bollymeter.basis: An 89% RT score from 62 critics who found it a thoughtful, well-acted Asimov riff - the show earns its premise through character rather than spectacle, though it rarely breaks beyond the philosophical territory it inherits from decades of AI fiction.

seasons.review_body: Humans premiered on Channel 4 in June 2015, adapted from the Swedish series Real Humans by Jonathan Brackley and Sam Vincent, and drew 5.4 million viewers in its opening week - the highest-rated new drama on Channel 4 that year. The 89-percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 62 critics reflected genuine appreciation tempered by the awareness that the show was working with well-trodden AI-consciousness territory. What distinguished it was the casting: Gemma Chan's Mia is the emotional centre of the Synth storyline, her restrained performance suggesting inner life without melodrama. Katherine Parkinson grounded the domestic subplot in something recognisably human. The Hollywood Reporter called it a keeper. Critics noted it asked real questions about personhood, consent, and labour without fully answering any of them - a feature in 2015, a mild frustration by Season 3.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere builds the Synth world in the background while keeping the foreground domestic and recognisable: a family buying an android helper and discovering that the product they purchased is more than the catalogue described. The show's restraint in its pilot is its biggest early achievement - it does not rush to declare what it is, letting the uncanny accumulate.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Anita's eyes in the kitchen at night - the moment the show commits to the idea that this is not a horror story but something harder to classify.

bollymeter.basis: 94% on RT from 17 critics with the consensus that it quietly distinguishes itself from flashier AI competition - the show broadened its societal focus and the Synth ensemble became stronger as individual characters developed.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 aired on Channel 4 in October 2016 and earned 94-percent Rotten Tomatoes approval from 17 critics, with the consensus that the show continued to distinguish itself through character rigour rather than spectacle. The Synth civil rights framing - conscious Synths navigating a world designed to deny their personhood - moved to the foreground. Gemma Chan and Colin Morgan anchored the Synth storylines while the Hawkins family remained the human access point. The season benefited from the writers having established the world rules in Season 1 and using Season 2 to push against them. The 86-percent audience score on Rotten Tomatoes held strongly. Critics noted the show was doing quieter work than most AI dramas of the period and valued it for that restraint.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 expands the societal dimension of the Synth consciousness question and gives the non-human characters more structural weight than the domestic household storyline.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on RT from 13 critics, though the audience score dropped to 78% - the sociopolitical ambition of the final season outpaced its narrative resolution, and cancellation before the story completed left the show without the closing argument it had earned.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 aired from May 2018 on Channel 4 with a perfect 100-percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 13 critics, who found the season's expanded sociopolitical scope - Synths integrated into and then violently expelled from public life - its most ambitious storytelling yet. The show used immigration policy, identity documentation, and labour rights as its real-world analogues without becoming a parable. Audience scores at 78 percent on Rotten Tomatoes reflected a viewer base with mixed feelings about the closing arc: the season ends without resolution because Channel 4's cancellation was announced mid-story. The show's critical consensus praised the new societal dimensions and the deepening character work; audiences were more frustrated that three seasons of careful world-building ended without the ending it earned.
seasons.season_over_season: The most sociopolitically engaged season and arguably the most ambitious; the cancellation truncated an arc that critics felt deserved completion.
